source.title: Feature-Learning Networks Are Consistent Across Widths At Realistic Scales
source.authors: Nikhil Vyas; Alexander Atanasov; Blake Bordelon; Depen Morwani; Sabarish Sainathan; Cengiz Pehlevan

record.tranche_reason: The study fits loss against network width and reports task-dependent fitted exponents. This refines the scope of scaling claims, but it does not test the original parameter/token/compute scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports training-loss behavior across widths and power-law fits versus width. It does not report held-out pretraining loss scaling against parameter count, tokens, or compute; those results do not test V1–V3. Its vision and language experiments do not test whether the same power law holds across modalities or regimes as stated in V5, nor downstream predictability as stated in V6. Values cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own loss-versus-width curves, Loss = C·N^-β + D, for a µP transformer on Wikitext-103 and a µP ResNet-18 on ImageNet, and compares the fitted exponents across tasks. Training is online (single pass, no repeated data), so training loss tracks held-out loss. This is a new setting for model-size scaling (width sweeps in µP at fixed training duration), in language and in vision. It does not sweep tokens or compute and does not study allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find µP networks consistent across realistic widths, especially early in training, with finite-width deviations that grow with training time and task difficulty. They split these deviations into variance and a 'bias of narrower width'. They add that late-time training loss follows task-dependent power laws in width with exponents well below 1, so perturbation theory around the mean-field limit does not describe them.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares neural-network training loss across widths in µP, including vision and language tasks. It does not sweep parameter count, token count, or compute to fit the original language-model scaling laws.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed width consistency and deviations vary with task and training time; the study also reports differences between µP and standard/NTK parameterizations.

fits_no_version.finding: In offline multi-epoch training on noisy-label CIFAR-50k, ensembled narrower networks can outperform ensembled wider ones, breaking the 'wider is better' trend. On clean CIFAR-200k, train-loss bias and variance do not vanish with width.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under repeated data and overfitting, loss need not improve monotonically with model width.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted width exponents are far from the β=1 predicted by mean-field perturbation theory. Ensembles of narrow networks do not match a single wide network (finite-width bias).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Finite-width loss corrections at late training follow task-dependent exponents, not the universal 1/N.

record.problems: The numerical width-fit annotations are presented in Figure 9; the exact fit ranges and fit uncertainty are not stated. The reported fits concern training loss versus width, not held-out pretraining loss versus parameter count, tokens, or compute.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were included: the other loss-curve comparisons report width consistency or divergence but do not measure the versions' named parameter/token/compute scaling quantities.

untested.parts: Scaling in tokens or compute; loss against true parameter count; large LM pretraining scale. Only width at fixed training duration is swept, on a small 4-layer masked LM.
Not tested: no extrapolation from small fits to larger runs.
Not tested: depth and other shape choices are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Only the image classification width fit. Video, repeated-data scaling laws and fine-tuning or transfer laws are not tested.
Only dependence on task or dataset (and implicitly architecture). Parameter counting, schedule and fitting-method choices are not compared.

missing.what: Offline multi-epoch training (noisy CIFAR-50k) where ensembled narrower networks beat wider ones. This bears on whether monotonic size scaling survives repeated data.
Fit width range, number of widths per fit, and uncertainty on β are not stated, so exponents cannot be compared with confidence.

record.verdict_notes: I changed the record's V7 label from limits_scope to supports: V7 itself states that exponents depend on setup, so differing exponents support it. I linked r1 to V1 because the loss is measured in the online regime, where train loss approximates held-out loss; it remains a width-only, fixed-token, small-model result. I moved r2 from V1-type reading to V5 because it is vision. The study cites Kaplan and Hoffmann but is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute; the study reports training loss versus width.
Extrapolation from small runs to substantially larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes; the study's width comparisons do not test this claim.
Downstream-task performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.

The study compares task-dependent width exponents, but does not compare parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, compute-optimal splits, or held-out loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.

rows.subject: µP transformer on Wikitext-103
rows.size_stated: Width N; exact fit range not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit training loss against network width N after training
rows.note: The figure gives the fit annotation 6.95 × N^-0.42; the text states the fit form is Loss = C N^-β + D and reports R² above .99. The authors say the fitted width exponent is task-dependent.
rows.check: Training loss of a depth-4 masked-LM µP transformer, width 64–4096, after 1 online epoch. The fit is 6.95·N^-0.42 + D with R² > .99 (Fig. 9). Width N, not parameter count, is the variable. Parameters scale roughly as N², so the exponent in parameters is about 0.21. Tokens are fixed, so data may partly bottleneck. Baseline is the fitted offset D.

source_check.correct: Observed for V7; cannot_determine for V1. The measured quantity is online training cross-entropy versus width N, fitted as 6.95·N^-0.42 + D, with R² > .99. It does not directly measure V1's held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V7, but the row's V1 link does not match the specified measure and scaling coordinate.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 on ImageNet
rows.size_stated: Width N; exact fit range not stated
rows.operation_detail: Fit training loss against network width N after training
rows.note: The figure gives the fit annotation 11.2 × N^-0.63; the text states the fit form is Loss = C N^-β + D and reports R² above .99. The exponent differs from the Wikitext-103 fit.
rows.check: ResNet-18 on an ImageNet subset with heavy augmentation, trained for 2 epochs, so it is near-online rather than strictly online. The fit is 11.2·N^-0.63 + D with R² > .99 (Fig. 9). This is vision, not text, so it bears on V5 rather than V1. The variable is width (channels), not parameter count.

relation.reason: Section 4 fits loss-versus-width power laws and compares exponents across tasks, directly bearing on V5 and V7.

tranche.reason: Own width-scaling results in µP language and vision models test power-law form and task-dependent exponents in a new setting. The disagreement with a universal exponent concerns finite-width perturbation theory, rather than contradicting the catalog's claim versions.

source_check.notes: Figure 9 fits loss minus an estimated constant D, rather than an unshifted loss power law. The conclusion holds training time fixed and explicitly leaves joint width–training-time limits and compute frontiers untested.
